steps.title: The open
steps.content:
Hi, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. Is {{contact_first_name}} available, please?

Hi {{contact_first_name}}. We're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and yours came up. {{asked_by_provider}} I wanted to check that your home's plumbing is still doing what it should. Do you have a quick minute?

steps.title: The opening question
steps.content:
So {{contact_first_name}}, how has the plumbing been since we were last out? I usually hear one of three things. Still running great, starting to act up a little, or real problems. Which one is closest for you?

(Click the one you hear.)

steps.title: Still running great
steps.content:
That's great to hear, {{contact_first_name}}. That's what we like to hear.

While I have you, when was the plumbing last looked at or serviced?

(Let them answer. Click the closest one: recent, a while, or not sure.)

steps.title: Starting to act up
steps.content:
I appreciate you telling me that, {{contact_first_name}}. That does happen over time. The good news is you caught it while it's still small. Small things are a lot easier to fix than big ones.

(Let them respond.)

steps.title: Real problems
steps.content:
I'm sorry to hear that, {{contact_first_name}}. That's frustrating, and I'm glad we called when we did. What's been going on?

(Let them answer. Listen. Do not book anything yet.)

(Sewage backing up, a big active leak, flooding, or a gas smell: press the URGENT button.)

steps.title: Serviced recently
steps.content:
That's great, {{contact_first_name}}. Most people don't keep up with it, and it's why yours is still running well.

One more thing. Even with everything running well, have you noticed any small early signs? A drain that's gotten slow, a faucet that drips, or hot water that runs out sooner.

(Let them answer.)

steps.title: It’s been a while
steps.content:
About how long would you say?

(Let them answer.)

That's common. Plumbing just does its job, so time gets away from you.

Can I share why I ask?

(Wait for the yes.)

The longer plumbing goes without a look, the more likely something small is waiting to be found. A worn valve, a slow drip, a water heater full of sediment. Caught now, those are quick, cheap fixes. Small leaks alone can add to your water bill every month. Left alone, that small stuff turns into water damage or the emergency call. That never happens at a convenient time.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for the yes.)

Since it's been a while, I'd suggest we go through the plumbing in the home. The water heater, the drains, the shutoff valves. Then you know it's all in good shape. If it all looks great, that's good news too.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

(Things to note for the visit: whole-home inspection, water heater flush, maintenance agreement, main shutoff check.)

steps.title: Doesn’t know when it was serviced
steps.content:
No problem, most people don't keep track of that. Plumbing is out of sight, out of mind until something goes wrong.

Can I share why I ask?

(Wait for the yes.)

Two reasons. A slow drip or a running toilet adds to your water bill every month. That's money for nothing. And the bigger one. When a plumber catches a small problem early, it's usually a quick, cheap fix. The small stuff nobody catches is what turns into water damage or the emergency call. That never happens at a convenient time.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for the yes.)

Since nobody's sure where things stand, I'd suggest we give the plumbing a full check. The water heater, the drains, the shutoff valves. Then you know what shape it's all in. If it all looks great, that's good news too.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

steps.title: Maintenance plan
steps.content:
That's great that you're staying on top of it. You're ahead of most people.

Can I share a thought?

(Wait for the yes.)

The hardest part of taking care of plumbing isn't the service. It's remembering to schedule it. Life gets busy, a year slips by, and something small gets missed. With a regular plan you never have to remember. We remember for you. It stays on a schedule, and small things get caught before they turn into water damage.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for the yes.)

Since you're already taking care of the home, let us handle the regular plumbing checks from here. That way it's off your plate.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

(Things to note for the visit: whole-home inspection, water heater flush, maintenance agreement, main shutoff check.)

steps.title: The transition
steps.content:
Well {{contact_first_name}}, I'm glad we connected today. Can I ask you a few quick questions so I can update your service records?

(Wait for the yes.)

steps.title: Questions: update the records
steps.content:
Can I ask you a few quick things while I have you, {{contact_first_name}}?

(Ask one at a time. Note which ones come up. Do not dig into any single one yet.)

How's the hot water, does it run out sooner than it used to?

Any drains that are slow, or clogs that keep coming back?

Any faucets dripping, or toilets that run on their own?

How's the water pressure around the house?

How about the water itself, any taste, smell, or hard-water spots?

If you have a sump pump, when was it last tested?

And anything you've been living with, like a disposal that jams or a project you've put off?

So it sounds like the big ones are (the ones they named). Is that right?

Of those, which one bothers you the most?

(Tap the chip and click the button for the one they name.)

steps.title: Focus: water heater and hot water
steps.content:
That's the one we hear most, {{contact_first_name}}. Nobody should be rationing hot water in their own house.

Does it run out sooner, or take a long time to warm up?

(Let them answer.)

Do you know how old the water heater is?

(Age matters a lot here. Note their answers for the plumber.)

steps.title: Focus: drains and sewer
steps.content:
I'm glad you mentioned that, {{contact_first_name}}. The plunger treats the symptom, not the cause. When the same drain clogs over and over, something further down is catching things. It only builds.

Is it one drain, or more than one?

(Let them answer.)

How often is it happening now?

(More than one drain, or sewage smells, can mean the main line. Note it. Sewage backing up: press the URGENT button.)

steps.title: Focus: drips and running toilets
steps.content:
That little drip costs more than it sounds, {{contact_first_name}}. A running toilet alone can waste two hundred gallons a day. It all shows up on the water bill.

Is it a faucet dripping, or a toilet running?

(Let them answer.)

Has the water bill gone up without a clear reason?

(A higher bill with no visible leak can mean a hidden one. Note their answers.)

steps.title: Focus: water pressure and older pipes
steps.content:
That's a useful one to know, {{contact_first_name}}. Weak pressure is annoying, but it also tells us something. In an older home it can mean the pipes are narrowing from the inside.

Is it everywhere in the house, or just certain faucets?

(Let them answer.)

Do you know how old the home's plumbing is?

(Whole-house pressure loss in an older home is worth a real look. Note their answers.)

steps.title: Focus: water quality
steps.content:
I'm glad you brought that up, {{contact_first_name}}. You use that water for everything. Drinking, cooking, bathing the kids.

Is it more the taste and smell, or the hard-water side?

(Let them answer. Hard water means spots on dishes, scale on fixtures, soap that won't lather.)

(Hard water also shortens the life of the water heater and fixtures. Note their answers.)

steps.title: Focus: sump pump
steps.content:
I'm glad you mentioned that, {{contact_first_name}}. You usually find out a sump pump is broken on the worst possible day. Standing in a wet basement.

When was it last tested?

(Let them answer.)

Does it have a battery backup for when a storm knocks the power out?

(A pump test is quick, and it's the cheapest flood insurance there is. Basement flooding right now: press the URGENT button.)

steps.title: Focus: fixtures, disposal, and projects
steps.content:
That's good to know, {{contact_first_name}}. A disposal that's given up, a fixture past its prime, or a bathroom you've been planning. We help with all of it.

Tell me a little more. What have you been living with, or what's the project?

(Note the details. Projects are appointments, not phone quotes.)

steps.title: Making it real
steps.content:
(Three questions about the problem they named, in order.)

How long has that been going on, like a couple weeks, or since last season?

(Let them answer.)

Is it something you notice like 1 to 2 times a month, or is it more often than that?

(Let them answer.)

When it's at its worst, does it ever interfere with comfort at home, having people over, or the water bill?

(Let them answer. Repeat back whatever they name.)

Thank you for telling me that. Our plumbers see this all the time.

steps.title: Review and bridge
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, let me make sure I have this right.

(Read back their three answers: how long, how often, what it gets in the way of.)

So it started a while back, and it happens more than once in a while. At its worst it gets in the way of what you mentioned. Did I get that right?

(Say what they named: comfort at home, having people over, or the water bill. Let them answer. If they correct you, take the correction and move on.)

It sounds like you'd really like the plumbing to be something you never have to think about. Is that fair to say?

(Wait for the yes.)

steps.title: Recommendation
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, that's worth getting looked at instead of just living with it. Here's how this works. One of our plumbers comes out and takes a look at {{main_concern}}. While they're there, they give the home's plumbing a once-over. If anything else is going on, you'll know before it becomes a problem. If it all checks out, we'll tell you that too. Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for the yes.)

Let's get a plumber out to take that look. Does that sound reasonable?

(Say "reasonable", not "good". Click what you hear.)

steps.title: Uncover the real concern
steps.content:
I understand, {{contact_first_name}}. Can I ask what would keep you from taking care of something that's bothering you?

(Listen. Their real answer is almost always one of the buttons below.)

steps.title: Objection: cost
steps.content:
I understand, {{contact_first_name}}. This first step is just having a plumber take a look. You're not committing to anything today. Knowing where things stand is what protects you. The small stuff nobody catches is what gets expensive later.

(Do not quote prices or discounts. The office handles that.)

Would it be okay to at least get the look on the calendar?

(Wait for the yes.)

steps.title: Objection: “I need to think about it”
steps.content:
That's fair, {{contact_first_name}}. Can I ask which part you'd want to think over?

(Let them answer. Cost, timing, or not sure it's worth a visit. Their answer usually turns into one of the buttons below.)

The nice thing is, the visit is just information. Then you can think it over with real answers instead of guesses.

Does that sound fair?

steps.title: Objection: “I need to talk to my spouse”
steps.content:
That's fair, {{contact_first_name}}. Most people find it helps to have the plumber take a look first. That way you both have real information to decide with.

Would that work?

steps.title: Objection: too busy
steps.content:
I understand, {{contact_first_name}}. Life gets busy. You don't have to do anything for this one. Our plumber does the work, and we schedule it around you.

Is there a day that's usually easier for you?

steps.title: “Not interested”
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. I'm not calling to sell you anything today. We're updating our records on customers we haven't seen in a while. {{practice_name}} just wanted to make sure the plumbing is still treating you right. Can I ask one quick question?

(Wait for the yes.)

Is everything still running the way it should?

(A real question, asked warmly, re-opens most of these calls. Click what you hear.)

steps.title: Scheduling
steps.content:
Great, {{contact_first_name}}. We have time this week on (day) and (day). Do mornings or afternoons work better for you?

(Let them answer.)

Perfect. I have a (time) and a (time). Which is better?

(Let them answer.)

Great, I've got you down for (day) at (time).

(Have two days and two times ready before the call, both within 48 hours. Click what happens next.)

steps.title: Confirming the appointment
steps.content:
Perfect, {{contact_first_name}}. Let me confirm a couple of quick things. The best number to reach you is the one I called, right?

(Let them answer.)

And the address we have on file is still current?

(Let them answer.)

Will you be home for the visit, or should the plumber plan to meet someone else?

(Confirm phone, address, and who'll be there. Click what happens next.)

steps.title: Final discovery
steps.content:
One last thing, {{contact_first_name}}. Is there anything else around the house you'd like the plumber to look at while they're out? Even little stuff you've been putting off.

(Note anything they mention for the visit.)

steps.title: Close: appointment set
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, you're all set. Our plumber will take a good look at everything. If it all checks out, that's what we'll tell you. Thanks for your time today, and we'll see you soon.

(Add your notes and press the green "Scheduled" button below.)

steps.title: Close: callback set
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. When would be a better time for me to call you back?

(Pin down a real day and time. Do not settle for "sometime".)

Perfect, I'll call you then. Thanks, and have a great rest of your day.

(Add your notes, then press "Spoke. Call back later" below and pick the date they gave you.)

steps.title: Close: not now
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. I appreciate your time today. If anything ever comes up with the plumbing, you know where we are. Have a great rest of your day.

(Add your notes and log the call with the disposition that fits.)

steps.title: Voicemail
steps.content:
Hi {{contact_first_name}}, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. We're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and yours came up. Nothing urgent. I just want to make sure your home's plumbing is still running the way it should. Could you call me back at (your office number) when you have a few minutes? Again, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. Thanks, and have a great day.

(Press the "Voicemail" button below to log the call. The retry is scheduled automatically.)

steps.title: Someone else answered
steps.content:
Oh hi. This is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. We're updating our service records, and I was hoping to catch {{contact_first_name}} for a quick minute. Are they around?

(If they ask what it's about: "We take care of the plumbing at the house, and we're checking in on our customers." Keep it brief. No pitch.)

steps.title: “Why are you calling?” / “Is this sales?”
steps.content:
That's a fair question, {{contact_first_name}}, and no, I'm not selling anything today. We're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while. {{practice_name}} asked me to check that the plumbing is still treating you right. That's really it. So, how has it been holding up?

(Stay relaxed. Click what you hear.)

steps.title: Service recovery: they weren’t happy
steps.content:
I'm really sorry to hear that, {{contact_first_name}}, and I'm glad you told me. Can I ask what happened?

(Listen fully. Do not interrupt or defend. Let them get it all out.)

Thank you for telling me that. I'm going to make sure {{practice_name}} hears about it personally.

I know we can't undo that. I'd like the chance to make it right. Would you be open to letting us take another look? If you're not happy this time, you won't hear from us again.

(A real apology plus a low-risk offer wins back more customers than any discount.)

steps.title: They use another company now
steps.content:
That's fair, {{contact_first_name}}. I'm glad you've got someone taking care of it. Just for our records, was there anything about your experience with us that made you switch?

(Listen. If there was a problem, treat it as service recovery.)

I appreciate the honesty. If anything changes, or you'd like a second opinion on a big repair, we're here. Have a great day.

steps.title: They had the plumbing redone
steps.content:
That's great to hear, {{contact_first_name}}. New plumbing is a big investment in the house. Can I ask who did the work for you?

(If it was us, celebrate it. If not, stay warm.)

Even with new work, water heaters and drains still need an eye kept on them. Is anyone taking care of that for you?

(New work is a maintenance conversation, not a lost customer.)

steps.title: Moved, renting, or property changes
steps.content:
Thanks for letting me know, {{contact_first_name}}. Just so I update our records right, did you move, or is the property rented out now?

(Moved: wish them well, ask if the new owner might want our info, and log the call.)

(Landlord: they still own the plumbing. Keep going about keeping it in good shape between tenants.)

steps.title: Wrong number
steps.content:
I apologize for the confusion. I was trying to reach {{contact_first_name}}. Sorry to bother you, and have a great day.

(Log the call with a note that the number is wrong so we don't call it again.)

steps.title: “Don’t call me again”
steps.content:
I understand, and I'll take care of that right now. You won't hear from us again. Thank you for your time, and have a good day.

(Press the "Do Not Call" button below right away. This is a legal requirement.)

steps.title: URGENT: safety first
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, stop me right there. Let's take care of you first.

If you smell gas, please hang up with me now. Get everyone out of the house. Then call your gas company's emergency line or 911.

If sewage is backing up or water is flooding, shut off the main water valve. Only if you can reach it safely. We'll get a plumber out to you as an emergency call today.

(Follow your company's emergency dispatch procedure. Do not continue this script.)
